title: The Shub–Smale τ-conjecture: polynomially many integer roots from short arithmetic programs
formal: Does there exist an absolute constant C≥1 such that, for every nonzero polynomial f∈Z[x], the number z_Z(f) of distinct integer roots satisfies z_Z(f)≤(1+τ(f))^C, where τ(f) is its minimum number of addition, subtraction, and multiplication operations starting only from 1 and x?
definitions: A straight-line program begins with registers containing 1 and the indeterminate x. Each subsequent register contains u+v, u−v, or u·v for two previously available registers; the two operands may be equal. Previously computed registers may be reused without restriction. A designated register must equal f as a formal polynomial over the integers. The cost is the number of arithmetic operations, and τ(f) is the minimum over all such programs. A zero-operation program may output 1 or x. No arbitrary integer constants are supplied: for example 2 must be built as 1+1, and all operations constructing other constants count. Division, comparisons, branching, and exponentiation as a primitive are forbidden. Multiplication counts even when both operands are constants; no bound is placed on intermediate degree or coefficient bit length. This is arithmetic operation count, not bit running time or formula size. Define z_Z(f)=|{a∈Z:f(a)=0}|; repeated roots are counted once. The zero polynomial is excluded. The same universal C must work for all f, regardless of degree, coefficients, or root magnitudes.
answer_criterion: Prove a polynomial bound with one absolute exponent C, or prove that no such exponent exists. A negative answer must yield polynomials violating every candidate polynomial exponent—for example, a family whose integer-root counts grow faster than every fixed power of their exhibited program lengths. One polynomial violating a proposed small exponent, or exponentially many real or complex roots, is insufficient. No uniform efficient procedure for finding the roots is requested.
context:
A short arithmetic program can represent an enormous polynomial. After s squarings, x^(2^s) has exponential degree although its computation has only s operations. Degree therefore gives only the elementary bound z_Z(f)≤2^τ(f). The conjecture says that distinct integer roots are much harder to pack into such a compressed representation than degree alone suggests. Multiplicity cannot replace distinctness: the same repeated-squaring example already has a root of exponential multiplicity.

The restriction to integer roots is substantive. Iterating q_0(x)=x and q_(j+1)(x)=q_j(x)^2−2 uses only a constant number of new operations per stage and gives 2^j distinct real roots for j≥1. Indeed q_j(2 cos θ)=2 cos(2^j θ), so the roots can be written down through distinct cosine values. Thus the unrestricted statement with real roots in place of integer roots is false. Conjectures about real roots of particular sparse sums of products impose additional circuit restrictions.

Shub and Smale connect a polynomial integer-root bound to P_C≠NP_C in the Blum–Shub–Smale model, where exact complex arithmetic has unit cost and branching tests equality. This explains why an apparently elementary univariate question belongs among fundamental complexity problems. The conclusion concerns computation over complex numbers; it must not be silently identified with a proof of Boolean P≠NP.

Rojas develops a p-adic approach, including a reduction showing that a polynomial bound only for integer roots congruent to 1 modulo one fixed prime would already imply the full conjecture. He also bounds rational roots by exp(O(s log(s+1))) in terms of additive complexity s, which charges additions and subtractions while allowing powers and multiplicative structure more freely. This is useful when additive complexity is small; it is not a polynomial bound in the full operation count τ.

The conjecture has consequences beyond the original machine model. Alekseev, Grigoriev, Hirsch, and Tzameret recall its implication for separating the constant-free algebraic classes VP^0 and VNP^0, and use it to obtain conditional lower bounds for a variant of the binary value principle in the Ideal Proof System over rational functions. These implications do not establish the conjecture, and their non-Boolean instances do not directly yield Frege lower bounds.

An August 2026 preprint reports exhaustive enumeration through eight operations, using the convention that −1, 0, and 1 are all free. Such a fixed change of constants can be simulated with constant extra cost in the model here, but exact small-length records depend on the convention. The computation is finite experimental evidence and has not been reproduced for this card; it cannot settle the existence of a universal exponent.
why: A precise number-theoretic route to major arithmetic circuit and algebraic machine lower bounds. It probes whether sharing intermediate computations can create many independent integer zeros cheaply, linking computational compression with arithmetic geometry and proof complexity.

importance.reason: A central arithmetic complexity conjecture with a very elementary statement and strong consequences for algebraic P versus NP and constant-free circuit lower bounds.

progress.text: Shub and Smale relate integer-root complexity to the intractability of complex polynomial feasibility and the separation P_C≠NP_C.
Rojas gives the fixed-prime digit reduction and exp(O(s log(s+1))) rational-root bounds in the different additive-complexity parameter. Neither proves a polynomial root bound in τ.
Alekseev, Grigoriev, Hirsch, and Tzameret publish conditional Ideal Proof System lower bounds from the τ-conjecture for a binary-value variant over rational functions.

Santibañez-Leal’s version 0.03 reports an exact census through eight operations in a convention with free −1,0,1. This finite computational claim is not independently reproduced here and gives no asymptotic resolution.

status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The universal integer-root bound remains unresolved in the sources reviewed. The August 2026 census is explicitly a finite computational claim, not a resolution. Full operation count, distinct integer roots, and the exclusion of the zero polynomial are fixed.
